questions.question: Which property changes when an origin moves a request from HTTP/2 to HTTP/3?
options: The business meaning of POST becomes idempotent
The framing, compression, security, and transport expression
Cache freshness becomes automatic
Authorization can be removed from the application
questions.explanation: HTTP semantics remain the application contract. HTTP/3 changes how the message is framed, compressed, protected, and transported over QUIC.

questions.question: Why can one lost TCP segment delay unrelated HTTP/2 streams?
options: Every HTTP/2 request uses the same stream identifier
HPACK disables retransmission
TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so later frame bytes wait for the missing range
HTTP/2 permits only one active response
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes logical streams, but all frame bytes share TCP's ordered delivery. A missing byte range prevents the parser from receiving later bytes for any stream.

questions.question: An application shell has 18 objects, but an HTTP/1.1 client admits at most 6 origin requests at once. What is the minimum number of admission waves in the lesson's model?
questions.explanation: ceil(18 / 6) is 3. The model separates this connection-pool queueing from the transport recovery behavior of a lost packet.

questions.question: What is the accurate HTTP/3 loss-recovery claim?
options: A lost request-stream packet does not directly block unrelated request streams, but congestion control still affects the connection
QUIC removes packet loss and congestion control
Every QUIC loss blocks every request stream until the connection restarts
HTTP/3 sends each request through a different UDP socket
questions.explanation: QUIC recovers stream data independently, so unrelated request streams can progress. Shared congestion, connection flow control, and critical control streams remain connection-wide concerns.

questions.question: Why does HTTP/3 use QPACK instead of applying HPACK unchanged?
options: QPACK removes all dynamic state
QPACK supports independently delivered QUIC streams and bounds field sections that wait for dynamic-table inserts
QPACK encrypts application content without TLS
QPACK replaces HTTP caching
questions.explanation: HPACK assumes the ordered delivery available on one HTTP/2 connection. QPACK separates table instructions so HTTP/3 can balance compression against blocked field sections under out-of-order delivery.

questions.question: Which statement matches current HTTP priority standards?
options: The original HTTP/2 dependency tree is mandatory for every server
Priority guarantees exact completion order across every intermediary
RFC 9218 provides urgency and incremental signals, but server scheduling must still be verified
HTTP/3 has no way to express priority
questions.explanation: RFC 9113 deprecated the original RFC 7540 priority scheme. RFC 9218 defines extensible signals, but they remain inputs to implementation-specific scheduling.

questions.question: A client learns h3 through Alt-Svc, but its network blocks UDP. What protects availability during rollout?
options: Remove the TCP listener after the first successful QUIC request
Keep HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 over TCP as a tested fallback
Increase the Alt-Svc cache lifetime immediately
Enable server push
questions.explanation: HTTP/3 discovery does not prove UDP reachability. A live TCP path lets the client continue over HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 when QUIC cannot establish.

questions.question: Why should an ordinary payment POST not be sent automatically in QUIC 0-RTT?
options: HTTP/3 cannot carry POST requests
Early data can be replayed, so the operation could create a duplicate effect without durable idempotency
TLS 1.3 does not encrypt early data
QPACK cannot encode POST fields
questions.explanation: 0-RTT data is encrypted but replayable. Unsafe operations should wait for handshake confirmation or use a durable idempotency contract that makes repetition harmless.
